subjects.name: Französisch
subjects.description: French is the most common second foreign language at German Gymnasien after English. It starts in Kl. 6 in most Länder (e.g. Bayern, Baden-Württemberg, Niedersachsen, Rheinland-Pfalz, Hamburg, Sachsen) and in Kl. 7 in NRW (G9), Hessen, Schleswig-Holstein and Berlin; in the Saarland and along the Rhine in Baden-Württemberg it is often the first foreign language. Learners reach about A2 by Kl. 8–9 and B1 by Kl. 10, and the Abitur in Grund- or Leistungskurs targets B2 (KMK Bildungsstandards fortgeführte Fremdsprache 2012). The DELF certificates are an optional extra.

subjects.name: Latein
subjects.description: Latin is chosen by many Gymnasium pupils as second foreign language, usually from Kl. 6 (e.g. Bayern, Baden-Württemberg, Niedersachsen, Hamburg, Sachsen, Saarland) or Kl. 7 (NRW G9, Berlin, Schleswig-Holstein); some schools teach it as first foreign language from Kl. 5, as third language from Kl. 8/9 or as a new subject in the Oberstufe. Three to four years of textbook-based language learning lead to the reading of original authors (Nepos, Caesar, Ovid, Cicero …) from Kl. 9/10. Depending on the Land, the Latinum (KMK agreement 2005) is awarded at the end of Kl. 10 or 11. Abitur requirements follow the KMK EPA Latein (2005); there are no KMK Bildungsstandards for Latin.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: French Sound–Spelling Links
topics.description: Read French words aloud from their spelling and spell words you hear, using the typical letter groups (ou, oi, eau/au, ai, eu, ch, gn, qu) and knowing that final consonants and final -e are usually silent. German learners must unlearn reading every letter.
evidence: Read unknown words with ou, oi, au/eau, ai, eu, ch and gn correctly aloud
Leave silent final letters unspoken (petit, grand, ils parlent) and say the h muet as nothing
Spell the French alphabet and write down short familiar words that are dictated
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads 'Mes trois oiseaux chantent' aloud, do they say the oi and eau sounds correctly and leave out the silent letters?

prerequisites.reason: English already showed that spelling and sound need not match one to one
Comparing sound systems of languages starts in primary school

topics.laenderNotes: In Länder where French is the first foreign language (Saarland, the Rheinschiene of Baden-Württemberg) this is already laid in primary school.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Nasal Vowels
topics.description: Hear, say and spell the French nasal vowels and tell them apart from vowel + n: blanc / blond / brin, bon / bonne. German has no nasal vowels, so learners must not pronounce the n.
evidence: Pronounce an/en, on and in/ain/un as nasal vowels without an audible n
Distinguish pairs such as vent – vont – vin when listening
Explain why the n is heard in bonne or une but not in bon or un
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} say 'un bon vin blanc' with four nasal vowels and no n sound at the end of each word?

prerequisites.reason: Nasals are spelt with the letter groups an, en, on, in, un
Practising sounds that German lacks is familiar from English th and w

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Liaison, Elision and Linking
topics.description: Link words the French way: obligatory liaison (les‿amis, vous‿avez), elision with an apostrophe (l'école, j'aime, c'est) and enchaînement across word boundaries, with the stress on the last syllable of the word group.
evidence: Make the obligatory liaisons after articles, pronouns and short adverbs (les‿enfants, ils‿ont, très‿important)
Write and say elided forms (l', j', d', n', qu') before vowels and h muet
Read a short dialogue with the stress at the end of each word group rather than on the first syllable
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} say 'les‿amis' with a z sound and write 'j'habite' with an apostrophe instead of 'je habite'?

prerequisites.reason: Liaison makes normally silent final consonants audible
Sentence stress and linking were first practised in English

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Accents and Cedilla
topics.nameDe: Akzente und Cedille (é, è, ê, ç, ë)
topics.description: Use and pronounce the French diacritics: accent aigu (é), grave (è, à, où), circonflexe (ê, â, î), tréma and cédille (ç), knowing that some change the sound (é/è, c/ç) and others mainly distinguish words (a/à, ou/où).
evidence: Pronounce é and è/ê differently and write them correctly in learnt words
Use ç before a, o, u to keep the s sound (français, garçon, nous commençons)
Tell minimal pairs apart in writing: a / à, ou / où, la / là
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} write 'Le garçon va à l'école' with the cedilla, the accent grave and the accent aigu in the right places?

prerequisites.reason: Accents modify the basic sound–letter rules

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Articles and Gender
topics.nameDe: Bestimmter und unbestimmter Artikel, Genus und Plural
topics.description: Use le/la/l'/les and un/une/des, learn each noun with its gender (masculin/féminin) and form the plural, including the contracted forms au/aux and du/des after à and de. French has two genders that often differ from German (la table – der Tisch).
evidence: Learn and use new nouns with their article and gender
Form the plural of nouns and use les/des, noticing that the -s is usually silent
Use au, aux, du and des correctly (au cinéma, le livre du professeur)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} say 'Je vais au collège' and 'la porte de la classe' with the right articles, not 'à le collège'?

prerequisites.reason: Grammatical gender and articles are known from German
Number is a familiar category

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Subject Pronouns, être and avoir
topics.description: Use the subject pronouns (je, tu, il/elle/on, nous, vous, ils/elles) with the irregular verbs être and avoir, including on for 'we' in speech and the choice between tu and vous.
evidence: Conjugate être and avoir in the present tense without help
Use on in everyday speech and ils/elles according to gender
Use avoir in fixed phrases where German uses sein (j'ai douze ans, j'ai faim)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} say 'J'ai douze ans' rather than 'Je suis douze ans'?

prerequisites.reason: Verb forms that change with the person are known from German
Learning an irregular 'to be' with pronouns was done in English

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Regular -er Verbs in the Present
topics.description: Conjugate regular -er verbs in the présent (parler, habiter, aimer) and notice that four of the six forms sound the same; handle the spelling changes of manger, commencer, acheter and appeler.
evidence: Write all present forms of a new -er verb correctly, including silent -e, -es, -ent
Hear that je parle, tu parles, il parle and ils parlent sound alike
Spell nous mangeons, nous commençons and j'achète correctly
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write 'ils jouent' with the silent -ent and explain why it is spelt that way although it sounds like 'il joue'?

prerequisites.reason: Subject pronouns are needed to conjugate
A present tense with person endings was learnt in English

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Verb Groups -ir, -re and Irregulars
topics.nameDe: Verben auf -ir und -re und häufige unregelmäßige Verben
topics.description: Conjugate the other verb patterns in the present: -ir verbs with and without -iss- (dormir, finir), -re verbs (attendre, vendre) and the high-frequency irregular verbs aller, faire, prendre, venir, pouvoir, vouloir and devoir.
evidence: Conjugate aller, faire, prendre and venir in the present tense
Use pouvoir, vouloir and devoir + infinitive to express ability, wishes and obligations
Sort new verbs into their group and conjugate a model verb of each group
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} say 'Nous faisons nos devoirs, puis nous allons au parc' with the correct forms of faire and aller?

prerequisites.reason: The -er pattern is the reference for the other groups

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Negation
topics.nameDe: Verneinung mit ne … pas, ne … plus, ne … jamais, ne … rien
topics.description: Negate sentences with the two-part negation around the conjugated verb (ne … pas, ne … plus, ne … jamais, ne … rien, ne … personne), with n' before a vowel and pas de instead of un/une/des.
evidence: Put ne and pas around the conjugated verb, also with an infinitive after it (je ne veux pas partir)
Use ne … plus, ne … jamais and ne … rien to express different meanings
Replace un/une/des by de after a negation (je n'ai pas de frère)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} say 'Je n'ai pas de chien' rather than 'Je n'ai pas un chien'?

prerequisites.reason: Negation is placed around the conjugated verb
English showed that negation can need extra words around the verb

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern already uses ne … plus, ne … jamais and ne … rien in Jgst. 6 and adds personne ne / rien ne in Jgst. 8.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Asking Questions
topics.nameDe: Fragen mit Intonation, est-ce que, Fragewörtern und Inversion
topics.description: Ask yes/no and information questions in the three registers of French: rising intonation (Tu viens ?), est-ce que, and inversion (Viens-tu ?), using question words such as où, quand, comment, pourquoi, qui, que/qu'est-ce que, quel/quelle.
evidence: Ask the same question with intonation, est-ce que and inversion
Use qu'est-ce que and quel/quelle correctly (Qu'est-ce que tu fais ? Quel âge as-tu ?)
Match the question form to the situation: intonation with friends, inversion in formal writing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} ask a French pupil what they do after school in two different ways, for example with 'Qu'est-ce que…' and with intonation?

prerequisites.reason: Questions are built around conjugated verbs
Question formation with an auxiliary was learnt in English

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Possessive and Demonstrative Determiners
topics.description: Use the possessive determiners, which agree with the thing owned rather than the owner (sa mère = seine/ihre Mutter), and the demonstratives ce, cet, cette, ces.
evidence: Choose mon/ma/mes, ton/ta/tes, son/sa/ses by the gender and number of the noun
Use mon/ton/son before a feminine noun starting with a vowel (mon amie)
Use ce, cet, cette and ces correctly (cet hôtel, cette année)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} say 'sa sœur' for both 'seine Schwester' and 'ihre Schwester' and 'mon école' rather than 'ma école'?

prerequisites.reason: Determiners agree with the noun's gender and number
Pronoun and determiner forms are known from German

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Adjective Agreement and Position
topics.description: Make adjectives agree in gender and number with their noun (petit – petite – petits – petites, including the irregular beau/belle, nouveau/nouvelle, vieux/vieille) and place them after the noun, except a small group of short frequent adjectives that come before it.
evidence: Write feminine and plural forms of regular and common irregular adjectives
Place most adjectives after the noun and grand, petit, beau, bon, jeune, vieux before it
Hear the difference where agreement is audible (petit / petite, blanc / blanche)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} write 'une petite maison blanche' with both adjectives agreeing and in the right place?

prerequisites.reason: Agreement follows the noun's gender and number
The word class adjective is known from German

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Near Future and Recent Past
topics.nameDe: Futur composé (aller + Infinitiv) und passé récent (venir de)
topics.description: Talk about plans with the futur composé (Je vais visiter Paris) and about something that has just happened with venir de + infinitive (Il vient de partir).
evidence: Form the futur composé with the present of aller and an infinitive
Describe plans for the weekend or holidays with the futur composé
Use venir de + infinitive to say that something has just happened
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you three things they are going to do next weekend using 'je vais' + infinitive?

prerequisites.reason: Needs the present tense of aller and venir
English going to is built the same way

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Partitive Article and Quantities
topics.nameDe: Teilungsartikel und Mengenangaben (du, de la, beaucoup de)
topics.description: Use the partitive article for an unspecified amount (du pain, de la confiture, de l'eau, des pommes), which German leaves out, and de after expressions of quantity and negation (un kilo de, beaucoup de, pas de).
evidence: Use du, de la, de l' and des when talking about food in unspecified amounts
Use de alone after quantities (une bouteille d'eau, trop de sucre)
Explain the difference between 'J'aime le chocolat' and 'Je mange du chocolat'
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes a shopping list in French, do they write 'un kilo de tomates' and 'du fromage' correctly?

prerequisites.reason: Partitive forms combine de with the definite article
pas de follows the same rule as quantities

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Jgst. 7 together with en partitif; BW Kl. 6–8; the Niedersachsen KC 2025 has quantities with de only by Kl. 9.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Passé Composé with avoir and être
topics.nameDe: Passé composé mit avoir und être
topics.description: Talk about completed past events with the passé composé: auxiliary avoir or être plus past participle, using être with verbs of movement/change of state and reflexive verbs, where the participle agrees with the subject (elle est partie).
evidence: Form regular and common irregular participles (parlé, fini, vendu, fait, pris, eu, été, vu)
Choose être for aller, venir, partir, arriver, rester, naître, mourir etc. and for reflexive verbs
Make the participle agree after être (elles sont arrivées, nous nous sommes levés)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell what they did last Saturday and say 'je suis allé(e)' but 'j'ai mangé'?

prerequisites.reason: Auxiliaries and participles build on present-tense verb knowledge
The German Perfekt with haben or sein works in a very similar way
Irregular past forms were already memorised in English

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Jgst. 7, BW Kl. 6–8 (second year), NRW Kl. 8 (French from Kl. 7); the Niedersachsen KC 2025 places it at the end of Kl. 9. Agreement with avoir is only receptive in Bayern Jgst. 8.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Direct and Indirect Object Pronouns
topics.description: Replace objects with the pronouns me, te, le, la, nous, vous, les (direct) and lui, leur (indirect), placed before the conjugated verb or before the infinitive, and in the passé composé with agreement of the participle after a preceding direct object (je les ai vues).
evidence: Choose le/la/les for direct and lui/leur for indirect objects (téléphoner à qn → je lui téléphone)
Place the pronoun before the verb, also in negation and with an infinitive (je ne la vois pas, je vais le faire)
Use object pronouns to avoid repetition in a short text
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} answer 'Tu as téléphoné à ta grand-mère ?' with 'Oui, je lui ai téléphoné' instead of repeating the noun?

prerequisites.reason: Pronoun position is also practised in the passé composé
Pronouns sit inside the ne … pas frame
Telling Dativ and Akkusativ objects apart prepares lui vs. le

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern: direct object pronouns Jgst. 6, indirect ones Jgst. 7, two pronouns together Jgst. 11; BW Kl. 6–8.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: The Pronouns y and en
topics.description: Use y to replace a place or à + thing (J'y vais) and en to replace de + noun or a quantity (J'en veux deux), placed like the other object pronouns.
evidence: Replace à + place or thing with y (Tu vas à Paris ? – Oui, j'y vais)
Replace a partitive or quantity with en and keep the number (J'en ai trois)
Place y and en correctly in negative sentences and the passé composé (Je n'en ai pas mangé)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} 'Tu as des frères ?', can they answer 'Oui, j'en ai deux' using en?

prerequisites.reason: y and en follow the same placement rules
en replaces partitive and quantity expressions

topics.laenderNotes: en partitif comes earlier (Bayern Jgst. 7), y and en as pronouns in Bayern Jgst. 9; BW uses them as chunks in Kl. 6–8 and introduces y fully only in Kl. 11.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: The Imparfait
topics.description: Form the imparfait from the nous-stem of the present (nous parlons → je parlais) and use it for descriptions, states and habits in the past (Quand j'étais petit, j'habitais à Lyon).
evidence: Form the imparfait of regular verbs and of être (j'étais)
Describe people, places and the weather in the past with the imparfait
Talk about past habits (Le dimanche, nous allions chez mes grands-parents)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} describe in French what their life was like when they were six, using the imparfait?

prerequisites.reason: The imparfait is introduced as the second past tense
The Präteritum is the German narrative past

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern introduces the imparfait in Jgst. 7 together with its opposition to the passé composé, BW in Kl. 6–8; NRW (French from Kl. 7) and Niedersachsen in Kl. 9.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Choosing Past Tenses in Narration
topics.nameDe: Erzähltempora: passé composé, imparfait und plus-que-parfait
topics.description: Tell a story by combining the tenses: imparfait for background and ongoing situations, passé composé for the events that move the story on, and plus-que-parfait for what had happened before. German does not mark this aspect difference.
evidence: Mark background (imparfait) and new events (passé composé) in a narrative text
Write a short story with both tenses (Il pleuvait quand soudain le téléphone a sonné)
Form the plus-que-parfait and use it for earlier events (Il avait déjà mangé quand…)
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} retells a story in French, do they use the imparfait for the background and the passé composé for what suddenly happened?

prerequisites.reason: Both past tenses must be formed before they can be contrasted
Anteriority is known from the German Plusquamperfekt

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern: opposition imparfait/passé composé Jgst. 7, plus-que-parfait Jgst. 8; BW: opposition Kl. 9/10, plus-que-parfait Kl. 11; NRW: second stage (Kl. 9–10).

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Relative Clauses
topics.nameDe: Relativsätze mit qui, que, où, dont, ce qui / ce que
topics.description: Join sentences with relative pronouns: qui for the subject, que for the direct object, où for place and time, later dont (de + noun) and ce qui / ce que for 'what'. French chooses by function in the clause, not by gender as German does.
evidence: Choose qui or que by asking whether the relative pronoun is subject or object
Use où for places and times (le jour où…) and dont with verbs taking de (le film dont je parle)
Use ce qui / ce que to say 'what' (Je ne sais pas ce que tu veux)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} complete 'C'est le garçon ___ habite à côté' and 'C'est le livre ___ je lis' with qui and que, and explain why?

prerequisites.reason: Subject–object distinction is practised with pronouns
Relative clauses are known from German

osMatches.note: os: relative clauses in English as first language

topics.laenderNotes: qui/que/où: Bayern Jgst. 7, BW Kl. 6–8, NRW first stage. ce qui/ce que: BW Kl. 9/10. dont and lequel: Bayern Jgst. 11, BW receptive Kl. 11.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: The Futur Simple
topics.description: Form the futur simple from the infinitive plus endings (je parlerai) and the irregular stems (ser-, aur-, ir-, fer-, viendr-, pourr-, voudr-), and use it for predictions, promises and plans further ahead.
evidence: Form the futur simple of regular verbs and the main irregular stems
Make predictions about the future (Dans vingt ans, j'habiterai…)
Use quand + futur where German uses the present (Quand je serai grand…)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} describe their life in twenty years in French using the futur simple, including 'je serai' and 'j'aurai'?

prerequisites.reason: Future reference is first expressed with aller + infinitive
The German Futur is a familiar comparison

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Jgst. 9, BW (G9) Kl. 9/10, NRW second stage; Niedersachsen (KC 2025) Kl. 10. The older BW G8 plan had it in Kl. 6–8.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Conditional and if-Clauses
topics.description: Form the conditionnel présent (futur stem + imparfait endings) for polite requests, wishes and hypotheses, and build the conditional sentence types: si + présent → futur, si + imparfait → conditionnel, and receptively si + plus-que-parfait → conditionnel passé.
evidence: Make polite requests and wishes (Je voudrais…, Tu pourrais… ?)
Build real and unreal conditional sentences with the correct tense pairs
Avoid the conditionnel after si (Si j'avais le temps, …, not 'Si j'aurais')
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} say what they would do if they won a trip to France, starting 'Si je gagnais…, je…'?

prerequisites.reason: The conditionnel uses the future stem
Its endings and the si-clause use the imparfait

externalPrerequisites.subject: Englisch
externalPrerequisites.concept: conditional sentences (if-clauses type I and II)
externalPrerequisites.reason: The tense pattern of if-clauses is usually learnt in English first

externalPrerequisites.subject: Deutsch
externalPrerequisites.concept: Konjunktiv II and würde-Form for unreal conditions
externalPrerequisites.reason: Unreal conditions are known from German

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Jgst. 9 (types I–III, conditionnel passé); BW Kl. 9/10 types I–II, type III in Kl. 11; NRW second stage; Niedersachsen Kl. 10.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: The Subjonctif Présent
topics.description: Form the subjonctif présent (stem of ils + -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent; irregular être, avoir, aller, faire, pouvoir, savoir) and use it after typical triggers: il faut que, vouloir que, emotions (je suis content que), and conjunctions such as pour que, avant que, bien que.
evidence: Form the subjonctif of regular and the main irregular verbs
Use it after il faut que, vouloir que and expressions of feeling
Decide between indicative and subjonctif after expressions of opinion and certainty (je pense que / je ne pense pas que)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} complete 'Il faut que tu … (faire) tes devoirs' and 'Je veux que vous … (venir)' with the subjonctif?

prerequisites.reason: The subjonctif is built from present-tense stems
Learners already know that mood, not only tense, changes verb forms

osMatches.note: os: the subjunctive in English; the French subjonctif is far more frequent and trigger-based

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Jgst. 10; BW (G9) Kl. 9/10 after expressions of opinion and will; NRW second stage (Kl. 9–10); the Niedersachsen KC 2025 keeps it to chunks.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Reported Speech and Sequence of Tenses
topics.nameDe: Indirekte Rede und Zeitenfolge (concordance des temps)
topics.description: Report what someone said or asked (Il dit que…, Elle a demandé si…), changing pronouns, time expressions and, after a past introductory verb, the tenses (présent → imparfait, passé composé → plus-que-parfait, futur → conditionnel). French uses the indicative here, unlike the German Konjunktiv I.
evidence: Turn statements, yes/no questions and wh-questions into reported speech (si, ce que, où…)
Shift tenses correctly after a past introductory verb
Adapt time and place words (demain → le lendemain, ici → là)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} report 'Je viendrai demain', said by a friend yesterday, as 'Il a dit qu'il viendrait le lendemain'?

prerequisites.reason: Tense shifting needs imparfait and plus-que-parfait
The future in the past is expressed with the conditionnel

externalPrerequisites.subject: Deutsch
externalPrerequisites.reason: Reported speech is a familiar operation from German

osMatches.note: os: quoted and reported speech in English

topics.laenderNotes: Reported speech in the present comes early (Bayern Jgst. 7, NRW first stage); the shift of tenses comes in Bayern Jgst. 10 and NRW Kl. 9–10, in BW only in Kl. 12/13.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Gérondif and Present Participle
topics.description: Use the gérondif (en + -ant) to express simultaneity, manner or condition (Il travaille en écoutant de la musique) and recognise and use the participe présent as a written alternative to a relative or adverbial clause.
evidence: Form the -ant form from the nous-stem (en faisant, en finissant; irregular en étant, en ayant)
Express how or while something is done with the gérondif
Replace a qui-clause with a participe présent in formal writing and recognise it in texts
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} say how they learn vocabulary using the gérondif, e.g. 'J'apprends en écrivant les mots'?

prerequisites.reason: Both use the nous-stem of the present
The participle often replaces a relative clause

topics.laenderNotes: BW Kl. 9/10 (modal use), Bayern only in Jgst. 11; NRW lists participle constructions in the second stage.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Recognising the Passé Simple
topics.description: Recognise the passé simple as the written narrative tense of literature and fairy tales (il fut, elle eut, ils arrivèrent) and understand it as the literary counterpart of the passé composé; active use is not required.
evidence: Identify passé simple forms in a literary text and name their infinitive
Recognise the frequent irregular forms (fut, eut, fit, vint, dit, prit)
Explain why a novel uses the passé simple and a letter the passé composé
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads 'Il prit son manteau et sortit', can they say which verbs these are and that this is a literary past tense?

prerequisites.reason: Its role is understood by analogy with the narrative tenses

topics.laenderNotes: Receptive only: Bayern Jgst. 10, NRW second stage, BW only in Kl. 12/13.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Numbers, Time and Dates
topics.description: Use French numbers including the tricky 70–99 (soixante-dix, quatre-vingts, quatre-vingt-dix), tell the time, and give dates, prices and phone numbers in the French way.
evidence: Say and understand numbers up to 1000, including 70–99
Tell the time in everyday and official form (trois heures et quart / quinze heures quinze)
Give dates and birthdays (le 14 juillet, le premier mai) and read prices in euros
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read out the French phone number 06 78 91 74 85 in pairs of digits, as French people do?

prerequisites.reason: Telling the time in a foreign language was practised in English
Numbers show liaison and silent letters (six, dix, vingt)

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: School and Daily Routine
topics.description: Talk about school subjects, the timetable, the classroom and one's daily routine, including the reflexive verbs of the routine (se lever, se laver, s'habiller).
evidence: Name school subjects, rooms and objects and say which subjects they like
Describe their daily routine with times and reflexive verbs (Je me lève à sept heures)
Understand and use the main classroom phrases (Je n'ai pas compris, Comment dit-on… ?)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} describe a normal school day in French from getting up to going to bed?

prerequisites.reason: Routines are described with present-tense verbs
Times structure the daily routine

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Food, Meals and Shopping
topics.description: Use the vocabulary of food, French meals (petit-déjeuner, déjeuner, goûter, dîner), markets and shops, quantities and prices.
evidence: Name common foods and drinks and say what they eat at each French meal
Buy food at a market or boulangerie using quantities and prices
Read a simple recipe or menu and order a meal
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} buy a baguette, two croissants and 500 grams of cheese in a French role play, asking the price?

prerequisites.reason: Food vocabulary is used with partitive and quantities
Prices and quantities need numbers

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Leisure, Media and Travel
topics.description: Talk about hobbies, sport, music, media use, holidays and travel (transport, accommodation, weather, sights), the topic areas of the second and third year of French.
evidence: Describe their hobbies and media habits and ask others about theirs
Talk about a past holiday: destination, transport, accommodation, activities
Use weather and travel vocabulary to plan a trip
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell a French exchange partner in a few sentences where they went on holiday, how they got there and what they did?

prerequisites.reason: Holiday reports use the passé composé
Extends the first personal vocabulary fields

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Greeting and Introducing Oneself
topics.description: Greet, introduce yourself and your family and friends, and ask others about themselves, choosing tu or vous and the right greeting (Salut, Bonjour Madame, la bise).
evidence: Introduce themselves with name, age, home town, family and pets
Ask a partner the same questions and react to the answers
Choose tu or vous and the greeting according to the person (friend, teacher, stranger)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} introduce themselves and their family to a French host family, saying 'vous' to the parents and 'tu' to the children?

prerequisites.reason: Introductions use être and avoir (je suis, j'ai… ans)
Introductions were the first speaking task in English too

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Communication Strategies
topics.description: Keep a conversation going despite gaps: ask for repetition or explanation (Pardon ? Tu peux répéter ? Ça veut dire quoi ?), paraphrase missing words (C'est un truc pour…), use gestures and fillers (euh, alors, bon).
evidence: Ask for repetition, slower speech or an explanation in French
Paraphrase a word they do not know (c'est quelqu'un qui…, c'est le contraire de…)
Use fillers and short reactions to gain time and show interest
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} does not know the French word for 'Regenschirm', can they still explain what they mean in French?

prerequisites.reason: The same strategies were practised in English
Strategies are used from the first conversations on

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Everyday Transactions in France
topics.nameDe: Alltagssituationen bewältigen (einkaufen, bestellen, nach dem Weg fragen)
topics.description: Manage short service conversations in France: shopping, ordering in a café, asking for and giving directions, buying tickets and asking for information, using polite forms.
evidence: Order food and drink and ask for the bill politely
Ask for and give directions in a town using a map
Buy a train or metro ticket and ask for times and platforms
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} ask a passer-by in French how to get to the station and understand the answer?

prerequisites.reason: Service conversations need the vocabulary of food, shops and prices
Requests and information questions are needed
Similar role plays were done in English

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Giving a Short Talk
topics.description: Give a prepared short talk of a few minutes in French on a familiar topic (a region, a francophone star, a hobby), speaking freely from notes and using simple visual support.
evidence: Prepare a structured talk with introduction, main part and conclusion
Speak from keyword notes rather than reading a text
Answer simple questions from classmates after the talk
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} talk for two minutes in French about a French region using only a card with keywords?

prerequisites.reason: Short presentations were first given in English
Presentation techniques are known from Deutsch
Topics come from the familiar vocabulary fields

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Giving and Defending Opinions
topics.description: Take part in a discussion on familiar topics (school, media, environment): give and justify opinions, agree and disagree politely and react to others' arguments.
evidence: Express an opinion with reasons (À mon avis…, parce que…, d'abord… ensuite…)
Agree and disagree politely (Je suis d'accord, mais…, Je ne suis pas de ton avis)
Respond to a partner's argument with a counter-argument
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a class discussion on whether mobile phones should be banned at school, can {{name}} give their opinion in French and answer a counter-argument?

prerequisites.reason: Discussion needs strategies for gaps and turn-taking
Opinion phrases partly require the subjonctif
Structured speaking is practised first in prepared talks

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Presenting and Commenting on a Text
topics.nameDe: Textvorlagen mündlich vorstellen und Stellung nehmen
topics.description: In the Oberstufe and its oral exam (mündliche Prüfung or Kommunikationsprüfung), present a text, picture or topic coherently, summarise its message and take a reasoned position on the issue it raises.
evidence: Present the content and message of a text or cartoon in a few structured minutes
Take and justify a personal position on the issue raised
Answer follow-up questions spontaneously in a discussion
topics.assessmentPrompt: Given a short article on youth unemployment in France, can {{name}} present it in French for three minutes and then defend their own view?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on giving and defending opinions
Builds on prepared talks

topics.laenderNotes: Many Länder replace one written exam in the Oberstufe with an oral communication exam (e.g. NRW mündliche Prüfung in der Q-Phase, Bayern Kolloquium/Sprechfertigkeitsprüfung).

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Understanding Everyday Spoken French
topics.description: Understand classroom French, textbook dialogues, short messages and announcements (gare, supermarché), listening either for the gist or for specific information such as times, prices and places.
evidence: Follow instructions given in French in class
Extract times, platforms or prices from a station or shop announcement
Say who is talking, where, and what about after listening to a short dialogue
topics.assessmentPrompt: After hearing a French station announcement once, can {{name}} say which platform and at what time the train to Lyon leaves?

prerequisites.reason: Global and selective listening strategies were learnt in English
Announcements are full of numbers and times

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Chansons, Clips and Short Films
topics.description: Understand the main ideas, characters and mood of French chansons, YouTube clips, news for young people (e.g. 1jour1actu) and short films, using images and music as support.
evidence: Summarise the story and main message of a chanson or clip
Describe the characters and mood of a short film scene
Relate what is heard to what is seen to fill comprehension gaps
topics.assessmentPrompt: After watching a French short film twice, can {{name}} tell you in German or French what happens and how the main character feels?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on listening strategies with simpler texts
Audiovisual comprehension was practised in English

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Authentic Audio and Video Media
topics.nameDe: Authentische Hör- und Hörsehtexte (Radio, Podcast, Nachrichten)
topics.description: Understand authentic French radio and TV reports, podcasts, interviews and feature films on social topics at about B2 level, including speakers' attitudes and the cultural context.
evidence: Extract main points and details from an authentic report or podcast according to a task
Identify speakers' attitudes and moods in an interview
Link the information to background knowledge about France
topics.assessmentPrompt: After listening to a French radio interview about the baccalauréat, can {{name}} say what the interviewee criticises and how they feel about it?

prerequisites.reason: Extends audiovisual comprehension to authentic, faster texts

topics.laenderNotes: A listening or listening-viewing task is part of the written Abitur in several Länder (e.g. via the IQB pool) or is assessed in class tests.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Understanding Regional and Fast Speech
topics.nameDe: Regionale und frankophone Varietäten und schnelles Sprechen verstehen
topics.description: Understand the essentials of French spoken fast, informally or with regional and francophone accents (Québec, West Africa, Belgium, the Midi), as in films, interviews and street conversations.
evidence: Follow the gist of a film scene with fast, informal speech
Understand the main points of speakers from Québec or West Africa
Name typical features of a variety they heard (e.g. Québec diphthongs, 'septante' in Belgium)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Watching an interview with a Québécois speaker, can {{name}} still say what the main points were?

prerequisites.reason: Requires secure comprehension of standard authentic speech
Knowledge of registers and varieties helps to decode them

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Reading Everyday and Factual Texts
topics.description: Read short everyday texts (messages, posters, menus, timetables, blog posts) and simple factual texts, skimming for the gist and scanning for specific information.
evidence: Find specific information in a timetable, programme or advert
State the main idea of a short factual text or blog post
Answer comprehension questions about a textbook text without translating it word by word
topics.assessmentPrompt: Given a French cinema programme, can {{name}} quickly find when a certain film starts and how much a ticket costs?

prerequisites.reason: Skimming and scanning were learnt in English
Decoding French spelling supports reading

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Reading a Youth Novel
topics.description: Read a longer text, such as a simplified reader or an authentic youth novel, following the plot over several chapters and responding to the characters and themes.
evidence: Summarise the plot of each chapter in a few sentences
Describe the main characters and how they change
Express and justify their own reaction to the story
topics.assessmentPrompt: After reading a French youth novel, can {{name}} explain in French what the main character's problem is and how it is resolved?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on reading strategies with short texts
Narratives use the past tenses
Inferring unknown words keeps longer reading going

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern reads excerpts of a youth novel in Jgst. 10 and a complete one in Jgst. 11.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Reading Press Articles
topics.description: Read authentic press texts (Le Monde, Libération, Le Figaro, regional papers) on social and political issues, distinguishing report from opinion and recognising implicit statements and the writer's intention.
evidence: Tell a news report, an interview and an editorial (éditorial, tribune) apart
Identify the main thesis and supporting details of an article
Recognise implicit attitudes and the intended effect on readers
topics.assessmentPrompt: Given an editorial from a French newspaper, can {{name}} say what the author's opinion is and how they try to convince the reader?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on reading strategies for factual texts
Longer sustained reading is practised first with a novel

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Messages and E-mails to a Pen Friend
topics.nameDe: Kurze Nachrichten, E-Mails und Briefe an Brieffreunde (corres)
topics.description: Write short personal messages, postcards and e-mails to a French pen friend (corres): introduce yourself, answer questions, invite and make arrangements, with the usual openings and closings (Salut, Bises, À bientôt).
evidence: Write an e-mail introducing themselves, their family and hobbies
Answer the questions in a received message and ask questions back
Use informal openings and closings correctly
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write a first e-mail to a French exchange partner that introduces themselves and asks three questions?

prerequisites.reason: The content of first messages is the self-introduction
Short e-mails were first written in English

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Writing Stories and Reports of Experiences
topics.description: Write connected narrative texts in French: a report of a weekend or exchange, a diary entry, or a short story continuing a textbook text, using time connectors and the past tenses.
evidence: Structure a narrative with time connectors (d'abord, ensuite, tout à coup, finalement)
Use imparfait and passé composé appropriately in their story
Write a diary entry that includes feelings and opinions
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write a short French story of about 150 words that starts with 'Il faisait nuit quand…'?

prerequisites.reason: Narratives need the imparfait alongside the passé composé
Builds on short personal texts
Narrative structure is known from Deutsch

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Writing an Opinion Text
topics.description: Write a short, structured opinion text or forum post on a familiar issue, giving arguments and examples and linking them with connectors (d'un côté… de l'autre, pourtant, c'est pourquoi).
evidence: State a clear opinion and support it with at least two arguments and examples
Link arguments with logical connectors
Write a reply to a forum post that takes up and answers its arguments
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write a forum post in French saying whether teenagers should have a smartphone, with two arguments and a conclusion?

prerequisites.reason: Opinion phrases are first practised orally
The structure of a reasoned opinion is known from Deutsch
Builds on writing connected texts

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Formal Letters and Applications
topics.nameDe: Formelle Briefe und Bewerbung (lettre de motivation, CV)
topics.description: Write formal letters and e-mails in French, for example an application for an internship or exchange (lettre de motivation, CV), using the French layout and set phrases (Madame, Monsieur, … Veuillez agréer…).
evidence: Lay out a formal letter the French way (sender, date, objet, formule de politesse)
Write a lettre de motivation for an internship or summer job
Switch register consistently from informal to formal (vous, polite formulas)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write a short French application for a summer job in a campsite, with the correct formal opening and closing?

prerequisites.reason: Contrasts with informal correspondence
Polite formal requests use the conditionnel

externalPrerequisites.subject: Deutsch
externalPrerequisites.reason: Application letters are first written in German

osMatches.note: os: formal vs informal register in English

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern: application for a holiday job Jgst. 10, applications for internships or study Jgst. 11; NRW: application and CV as target texts in the second stage and the EF theme Entrer dans le monde du travail.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Writing a Résumé of a Text
topics.description: Summarise the content of a French literary or non-literary text in your own words in a structured résumé: present tense, neutral tone, no quotations or personal opinion, as required in the compréhension part of the Abitur.
evidence: Name text type, author, title and topic in an introductory sentence
Reproduce the main ideas in their own words in a logical order
Keep to the present tense and a neutral tone without quotations or comments
topics.assessmentPrompt: Given a French newspaper article, can {{name}} summarise its main points in about 100 words in their own words?

prerequisites.reason: A summary needs full comprehension of the main points
Builds on writing structured texts

externalPrerequisites.subject: Deutsch
externalPrerequisites.concept: Inhaltsangabe zu literarischen und pragmatischen Texten
externalPrerequisites.reason: The Inhaltsangabe teaches the same principles in German

osMatches.note: os: summarising non-fiction in English as first language

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Writing an Argumentative Commentary
topics.description: Write an argumentative text on an issue raised by a source text (commentaire personnel, essai, lettre au rédacteur): develop a thesis, weigh arguments and counter-arguments with examples and reach a reasoned conclusion.
evidence: Plan a commentary with introduction, argument and counter-argument, and conclusion
Support each argument with examples, including from the source text
Use a range of connectors and set phrases of argumentation (certes… mais, en revanche, il en résulte que)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write a French commentary on whether the bac should be abolished, weighing both sides before giving their view?

prerequisites.reason: Extends the short opinion text into a full argumentation
Commentaries respond to an issue raised by a source text

externalPrerequisites.subject: Deutsch
externalPrerequisites.reason: Argument structure is taught in German

externalPrerequisites.subject: Englisch
externalPrerequisites.concept: writing a comment or argumentative essay
externalPrerequisites.reason: The same text type is practised in English

osMatches.note: os: persuasive writing in English as first language

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Creative Writing from a Text
topics.description: Explore a literary or film text by writing creatively from it: an inner monologue, a letter or diary entry of a character, a continued or changed ending, or a dialogue that fits the original.
evidence: Write an inner monologue or letter that is consistent with a character's situation and personality
Continue a text or rewrite a scene from another perspective
Keep register and style suited to the chosen text type
topics.assessmentPrompt: After reading a short story, can {{name}} write the diary entry of a minor character that fits what happened in the story?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on narrative writing
Creative tasks require understanding the characters

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Transforming Texts for New Readers
topics.nameDe: Texte umgestalten und für andere Adressaten adaptieren
topics.description: Transform a source text into a different text type, register or period: turn a literary scene into a news article, an older text into modern French, or a specialist text into a version for younger readers, with deliberate reader guidance.
evidence: Adapt content, register and layout of a text for a new audience
Convert a text into another text type with its conventions (e.g. article, speech, blog)
Explain the changes they made and why
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} rewrite an excerpt from a 19th-century French novel as a modern blog post for teenagers and explain their choices?

prerequisites.reason: Requires confident creative text production
Adapting to a new audience means changing register

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Mediating in Everyday Situations
topics.description: Help people who do not share a language by passing on the gist, not a word-for-word translation: explain a French menu or sign to your family, or tell a French guest what a German announcement means.
evidence: Pass on the relevant information of a French text or conversation in German
Explain German information to a French speaker in simple French
Leave out unimportant details and paraphrase words they do not know
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a French restaurant, can {{name}} explain to their German-speaking grandparents what the dishes on the menu are?

prerequisites.reason: Mediation happens in the same everyday situations
Everyday mediation was first practised in English

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Written Mediation of German Texts
topics.description: Convey the relevant content of a German text (article, flyer, website) in French for a given French addressee and purpose, in a set text type such as an e-mail or blog post, selecting and paraphrasing instead of translating.
evidence: Select the information that the task and the addressee require
Render it in French in their own words and in the required text type
Use compensation strategies (paraphrase, examples) for words they lack
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write an e-mail in French telling a French friend the key points of a German article about school exchange programmes?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on oral everyday mediation
Mediation results are written as e-mails or posts

topics.laenderNotes: Sprachmittlung is a compulsory part of the written Abitur in French in many Länder (e.g. NRW, Niedersachsen; IQB task pool).

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Mediating with Cultural Explanations
topics.description: When mediating complex texts, add the explanations a French addressee needs to understand German realities (Abitur, Kita, Föderalismus, duale Ausbildung) and handle the two languages creatively where no direct equivalent exists.
evidence: Identify culture-specific terms in a German text that a French reader would not understand
Add short explanations or French comparisons (l'Abitur, l'équivalent du bac)
Justify which information they adapted, added or left out for the addressee
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} mediates a German text about vocational training for a French reader, do they explain what an 'Ausbildung im dualen System' is?

prerequisites.reason: Requires secure written mediation
Knowing both societies shows where explanations are needed

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Everyday Life and School in France
topics.nameDe: Alltag und Schule in Frankreich (collège, lycée, cantine)
topics.description: Know how French teenagers live and go to school (collège and lycée, the class numbering 6e–terminale, all-day school, the cantine, mercredi après-midi, the bac) and compare it with your own life in Germany.
evidence: Describe the French school system and the numbering of classes from 6e to terminale
Compare a French and a German school day
Know everyday customs such as la bise and meal times and use them in role plays
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain to you what a French 'élève de quatrième' does on a typical school day and what is different from their own school?

prerequisites.reason: Comparison needs the vocabulary of school and routine
Comparing school life abroad was done for Britain

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Paris
topics.description: Know the main sights and quarters of Paris (Tour Eiffel, Louvre, Notre-Dame, Montmartre, the Seine, arrondissements), find your way with the métro plan, and understand the city's central role in France.
evidence: Name and locate at least six sights of Paris on a map
Plan a route across Paris with the métro plan and describe it in French
Explain why so much of French political, economic and cultural life is concentrated in Paris
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} plan a day in Paris with three sights and explain which métro lines to take between them?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on the first picture of everyday life in France
Capitals and countries of Europe are known from Erdkunde

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern meets Paris in Jgst. 6 and compares Paris, Lyon, Nantes and Brittany in Jgst. 7; BW expects at least three major French cities by Kl. 8.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Regions of France
topics.description: Know the main regions and landscapes of France (e.g. Bretagne, Provence, Alsace, Île-de-France, the Alps) with their typical features, regional languages and cities, and the overseas territories (DROM).
evidence: Locate the main regions, rivers, mountains and cities on a map of France
Present one region with its landscape, economy, culture and regional language
Explain what the départements et régions d'outre-mer are
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} point to Brittany and Provence on a map and tell you two typical things about each region in French?

prerequisites.reason: Paris is the first place studied; the regions widen the picture
Map work on Europe is known from Erdkunde

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern: Brittany Jgst. 7, the régions Jgst. 8, Grand Est Jgst. 9; BW: one region by Kl. 8, the geography of France by Kl. 10, the administrative structure in Kl. 11.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: The Francophone World
topics.nameDe: La Francophonie: Französisch in der Welt
topics.description: Know where French is spoken beyond France (Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Québec, the Maghreb, West and Central Africa, the Caribbean), why (colonial history, international organisations), and learn about young people's lives in one francophone country.
evidence: Locate major francophone countries and regions on a world map
Explain in simple terms why French is spoken in these places
Present everyday life in one francophone country, e.g. Québec or Senegal
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} name five countries on three continents where French is spoken and explain why it is spoken in one of them?

prerequisites.reason: Extends knowledge of France to the wider francophone world
Information comes from factual texts

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern: Québec (partner province) Jgst. 8, Switzerland Jgst. 9, a Maghreb country Jgst. 10, Belgium Jgst. 11; BW and NRW require at least one francophone country or region in Sek I.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Franco-German Relations
topics.description: Understand how Germany and France moved from 'hereditary enemies' to partners: the wars of 1870–1945, the Élysée Treaty (1963) and the Aachen Treaty (2019), the Franco-German Youth Office (OFAJ/DFJW), town twinnings and exchanges; reflect on mutual stereotypes.
evidence: Outline the main stages of Franco-German relations since 1870
Explain what the Élysée Treaty and the OFAJ/DFJW do for young people (exchanges, Brigitte-Sauzay, Voltaire programmes)
Identify and question common German and French stereotypes about each other
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain in French why the Élysée Treaty of 1963 matters for school exchanges today?

prerequisites.reason: Comparisons of everyday life precede reflection on stereotypes
The EU frame of the partnership is known from Erdkunde

externalPrerequisites.subject: Geschichte
externalPrerequisites.concept: Franco-German reconciliation after 1945 and the Élysée Treaty
externalPrerequisites.reason: The historical background is taught in Geschichte

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Jgst. 9 (friendship, 22 January) and Jgst. 10 (Élysée and Aachen treaties); BW: an example of cooperation by Kl. 10, key dates of Franco-German history in Kl. 11; NRW Q-phase theme (R-)Évolutions historiques et culturelles. Saarland, Rheinland-Pfalz and BW link it to the border region.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Cities, Banlieues and Diversity
topics.nameDe: Ville et banlieue: Vielfalt, Migration und Integration
topics.description: Analyse life in French cities and their suburbs (banlieues): social housing, migration from the Maghreb and sub-Saharan Africa, discrimination and integration, and how films, rap and literature represent them.
evidence: Describe social and spatial contrasts between city centres and banlieues using texts and statistics
Explain the link between migration history and today's diversity in France
Compare the representation of the banlieue in a film, song or text with factual information
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain, using a scene from a banlieue film, which problems young people there face and how the film presents them?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on the first picture of Paris
Migration links France with the francophone world

externalPrerequisites.subject: Erdkunde
externalPrerequisites.concept: urbanisation and social segregation in metropolitan areas
externalPrerequisites.reason: Urban geography supplies the concepts

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern treats life in a large French city (housing, diversity) in Jgst. 10; BW: France as a multicultural society in Kl. 11; NRW Q-phase: culture banlieue, migration and integration.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Colonial Past and Postcolonial Francophonie
topics.description: Understand France's colonial empire and decolonisation (especially the Algerian War) and how this past shapes today's relations with the Maghreb and francophone Africa, debates on memory and identity, and francophone literature.
evidence: Outline French colonial expansion and decolonisation, including the Algerian War (1954–1962)
Explain how the colonial past affects present-day relations and debates in France
Analyse a francophone text or film from a postcolonial perspective
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why the Algerian War still matters in French society today, using an example from a text or film?

prerequisites.reason: Requires knowing where and why French is spoken
Migration in France is linked to the colonial past

externalPrerequisites.subject: Geschichte
externalPrerequisites.concept: European imperialism and decolonisation in Africa
externalPrerequisites.reason: The historical background is taught in Geschichte

topics.laenderNotes: NRW Abitur 2029 focuses on France and a sub-Saharan African country (colonial heritage); Bayern reads about a Maghreb country in Jgst. 10 and former colonies in the Oberstufe; BW Leistungs-/Basisfach theme La France et la francophonie dans un monde globalisé.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Reading Bandes Dessinées
topics.description: Read French comics (Astérix, Tintin, Le Petit Nicolas or modern BD) using their conventions: panels, speech and thought bubbles, onomatopoeia, image–text interplay, and the BD's place in French culture (Angoulême festival).
evidence: Explain how panels, bubbles and captions guide the reading of a BD page
Interpret onomatopoeia and visual signs (movement lines, symbols)
Write or complete the text of a short BD sequence
topics.assessmentPrompt: Given an Astérix page, can {{name}} explain how the pictures and bubbles together make a joke work?

prerequisites.reason: Reading the text of the bubbles requires basic reading skills

osMatches.note: os: how image order shapes meaning in English texts

topics.laenderNotes: NRW lists the bande dessinée in both Sek I stages; Bayern returns to the variety of francophone comics in Jgst. 10–11.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Analysing Narrative Texts
topics.description: Analyse French short stories, novels or excerpts (e.g. by Maupassant, Camus, Saint-Exupéry, contemporary authors): narrator and point of view (focalisation), characterisation, setting, structure and language, supporting the analysis with quotations.
evidence: Identify the type of narrator and focalisation and explain their effect
Characterise a figure using direct and indirect characterisation, with quotations
Use the French vocabulary of literary analysis (le narrateur, le point de vue, le champ lexical)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Given an excerpt from a French novel, can {{name}} write a paragraph analysing how the narrator presents the main character, with two quotations?

prerequisites.reason: Analysis builds on reading longer narrative texts
Narrator and perspective are introduced in Deutsch

externalPrerequisites.subject: Deutsch
externalPrerequisites.reason: The analytical categories are taught in German

osMatches.note: os: narrative perspective in English as first language

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Analysing Poems and Chansons
topics.description: Analyse French poems and song lyrics (e.g. Prévert, Baudelaire, Brel, contemporary rap and slam): structure, rhyme and the alexandrin, imagery and stylistic devices (procédés stylistiques), and how music and performance add meaning.
evidence: Describe form and structure of a poem or song (strophes, rimes, alexandrin, refrain)
Identify stylistic devices (métaphore, anaphore, énumération) and explain their effect
Relate lyrics, music and performance in an interpretation of a chanson
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how a repeated line in a Jacques Prévert poem or a Stromae song strengthens its message?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on understanding chansons
Basic terms of poetry are known from Deutsch

externalPrerequisites.subject: Deutsch
externalPrerequisites.reason: Poetry analysis is taught in German

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Film Analysis
topics.description: Analyse a French feature film or film sequence (e.g. Intouchables, La Haine, Les Choristes, Entre les murs): plot and characters, camera shots and angles, sound and editing, and how these film techniques create meaning.
evidence: Name shot sizes and camera angles in French (gros plan, plan d'ensemble, plongée) and their effect
Analyse how music, sound and editing shape a sequence
Interpret a key scene in relation to the film's theme
topics.assessmentPrompt: After watching a scene from a French film, can {{name}} explain why the director used a close-up at a key moment?

prerequisites.reason: Analysis builds on understanding films
Comparing book and film was started in Deutsch

externalPrerequisites.subject: Deutsch
externalPrerequisites.reason: Film terminology is introduced in German

osMatches.note: os: how images are framed, a simpler visual-literacy skill

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Analysing Non-fiction and Persuasive Texts
topics.description: Analyse French non-fiction texts such as articles, speeches, adverts and cartoons: structure of the argument, the author's intention, and the rhetorical and visual devices used to persuade, supported by references to the text.
evidence: Describe the structure of an argument (thèse, arguments, exemples, conclusion)
Identify rhetorical devices (question rhétorique, ironie, hyperbole) and their persuasive function
Analyse how text and image work together in an advert or cartoon
topics.assessmentPrompt: Given a speech by a French politician, can {{name}} show which devices the speaker uses to win over the audience?

prerequisites.reason: Analysis presupposes understanding the article
Knowing how arguments are built helps to analyse them

externalPrerequisites.subject: Deutsch
externalPrerequisites.reason: The categories are taught in German

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Interpreting Texts in Historical Context
topics.nameDe: Texte im historischen und gesellschaftlichen Kontext interpretieren
topics.description: Interpret French literary texts from different periods (e.g. Molière, Voltaire, Hugo, Camus) in their historical and social context, evaluate their devices and reflect on one's own interpretation process.
evidence: Use background knowledge about the period to explain a text's themes and intention
Evaluate how effectively stylistic devices serve the text's purpose
Reflect on how their first reading changed through contextual knowledge
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how a scene from a Molière comedy criticises the society of its time?

prerequisites.reason: Requires secure literary analysis
Older literary texts use the passé simple

externalPrerequisites.subject: Deutsch
externalPrerequisites.concept: literary epochs and their historical background (Aufklärung, Realismus)
externalPrerequisites.reason: Epoch knowledge is built in German literature lessons

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Learning French Vocabulary
topics.description: Learn and revise French vocabulary efficiently: with article and gender, in example sentences and word fields, with flashcards or apps and spaced repetition, including pronunciation and the spelling of silent letters.
evidence: Learn nouns with their article and verbs with an example sentence
Organise vocabulary in word fields, mind maps or a card system
Plan regular revision and check their learning with self-tests
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} show you how they learn their French vocabulary and why they always learn 'la' or 'le' with each noun?

prerequisites.reason: Vocabulary-learning techniques were developed in English

osMatches.note: os: vocabulary strategies in English as first language

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Using English, German and Latin for French
topics.nameDe: Mehrsprachigkeit nutzen: Wörter erschließen, false friends erkennen
topics.description: Use knowledge of English, German, Latin or a heritage language to infer French words (la nation, important, l'université), to recognise word-building patterns (-tion, -ment, -ité) and to watch out for false friends (la cave, le collège, actuel).
evidence: Infer the meaning of unknown French words via English, German or Latin
Recognise common French suffixes and prefixes and their English counterparts
Identify typical false friends between French, English and German
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out what 'la responsabilité' and 'internationale' mean without a dictionary, and explain how?

prerequisites.reason: False friends were first met between English and German
Inferring word meaning is practised in English
Language comparison starts in primary school

osMatches.note: os: Greek and Latin roots for English word meaning

topics.laenderNotes: Where Latin is the second and French the third foreign language (from Kl. 8 or 9), the Latin transfer is used systematically.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Using Dictionaries
topics.description: Use bilingual and later monolingual dictionaries (print and online) to find the right meaning, gender, conjugation and pronunciation (phonetic transcription); in the Oberstufe the dictionary allowed in exams is used efficiently.
evidence: Find the infinitive of a conjugated verb and look it up
Choose the meaning that fits the context among several entries
Read the phonetic transcription and grammatical information of an entry
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} looks up 'il faut', do they find it under 'falloir' and pick the right meaning?

prerequisites.reason: Dictionary skills were developed in English
Phonetic transcription is known from English
Look-up requires finding the infinitive of a conjugated verb

osMatches.note: os: dictionary use for spelling in English as first language

topics.laenderNotes: Which dictionary is allowed in tests and in the Abitur differs: many Länder allow a monolingual and a bilingual dictionary in the Abitur, some only a monolingual one.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Self-Assessment and the DELF
topics.description: Assess your own French against the CEFR levels (A1–B2) and prepare for the DELF scolaire, the official French certificate that German schools offer in cooperation with the Institut français, knowing its four skill papers.
evidence: Rate their own skills with CEFR descriptors or a language portfolio
Describe the four parts of the DELF exam (compréhension orale/écrite, production écrite/orale)
Complete a DELF practice paper at A2 or B1 level and evaluate the result
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} say which CEFR level they have reached in French listening and writing and what the DELF B1 would ask of them?

prerequisites.reason: Self-assessment with a language portfolio started in English
The oral exam includes a prepared monologue
The written exam asks for connected personal texts

topics.laenderNotes: DELF scolaire is optional and run by the Instituts français with the Länder ministries; schools typically offer A1 in the 2nd year, A2 in the 3rd, B1 in the 4th–5th year of French and B2 in the Oberstufe.

topics.subject: Französisch
topics.name: Registers and Varieties of French
topics.description: Recognise the registers of French (langue familière with verlan and youth slang, langue courante, langue soutenue) and regional and francophone varieties, and choose a register that fits the situation and text type.
evidence: Classify expressions by register (bouffer – manger – se restaurer; le mec, la meuf)
Rewrite a sentence from familiar into formal French
Name features of at least one regional or francophone variety
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why 'J'sais pas, c'est trop chelou' fits a chat with friends but not a letter to a teacher, and rephrase it formally?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on reflecting about language
The formal register is practised in formal letters

externalPrerequisites.subject: Deutsch
externalPrerequisites.reason: The concept of register is developed in German

osMatches.note: os: formal and informal English

topics.subject: Latein
topics.name: Reading Latin Aloud
topics.description: Read Latin aloud with the school pronunciation (c always as k, v as w, ae as ä) and the stress rules: two-syllable words on the first syllable, longer words on the penultimate if it is long, otherwise on the antepenultimate (Paenultima-Regel).
evidence: Pronounce c, v, ae, oe, qu and ti correctly in school pronunciation
Apply the penultimate rule to stress unknown words (amícus, dóminus)
Read a short Latin text aloud fluently with meaningful pauses
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads 'Caesar in Galliam venit' aloud, do they say 'Kaesar' and stress 'Gálliam' correctly?

prerequisites.reason: Comparing how languages sound starts in primary school

topics.laenderNotes: Most German schools use a 'restored' pronunciation with c = k; some teachers still use the traditional German pronunciation (c before e/i as z).

topics.subject: Latein
topics.name: Comparing Latin and German Structure
topics.description: Reflect on how Latin works differently from German and English: no articles, the subject hidden in the verb ending, cases instead of prepositions, flexible word order with the verb often at the end. Translating is therefore a constant comparison of two language systems.
evidence: Explain why 'Servus dominum vocat' and 'Dominum servus vocat' mean the same thing
Show where Latin uses a case ending and German a preposition or article
Name differences in tense use and word order between Latin, German and English
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why the Latin word 'laudo' needs three German words ('ich lobe' plus the missing subject) and why Latin needs no article?

prerequisites.reason: Comparing case systems requires knowing the German cases
German verb position is the reference for Latin word order
English fixed word order is a contrasting case

topics.subject: Latein
topics.name: Latin as a Base Language
topics.nameDe: Latein als Basissprache: Lehn- und Fremdwörter, romanische Sprachen
topics.description: Trace Latin in other languages: loanwords in German (Mauer, Fenster, Wein), foreign words and specialist terms (Präposition, Medizin, Aquarium), English vocabulary, and the Romance languages that developed from spoken Latin (French, Italian, Spanish).
evidence: Derive the meaning of German and English foreign words from Latin (Akkusativ, transport, captive)
Recognise Latin words in French, Italian or Spanish (aqua – eau – acqua – agua)
Explain the difference between a loanword and a foreign word
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain what 'portare' has to do with 'Porto', 'transport' and French 'porter'?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on the idea of word origin and language change
Needs a basic Latin vocabulary
Cross-language word comparison was met in English

osMatches.note: os: Greek and Latin roots for English word meaning, from the English side
os: Greek and Roman legacy including Latin roots

topics.subject: Latein
topics.name: Learning Latin Vocabulary
topics.description: Build and keep a basic Latin vocabulary by learning each word with its learning form: nouns with genitive and gender (rex, regis m.), verbs with their principal parts (do, dedi, datum), adjectives with all endings, revising in word fields and with spaced repetition.
evidence: Give the learning form of new nouns, verbs and adjectives
Use word fields and word families to organise and revise vocabulary
Keep up regular revision with a card system or an app
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you say 'rex' to {{name}}, do they answer 'regis, m. – der König' straight away?

prerequisites.reason: Vocabulary-learning techniques were developed in English

topics.laenderNotes: Plans differ in size and naming of the basic vocabulary (e.g. around 1,200–1,500 words by the end of the language course; Bayern works with a fixed Grundwortschatz).

topics.subject: Latein
topics.name: Latin Word Formation
topics.description: Infer the meaning of unknown Latin words from their parts: prefixes (ad-, con-, de-, ex-, in-, re-) with assimilation (ad + fero → affero), suffixes (-tor, -tas, -io, -bilis, -osus) and word families (amare – amicus – amicitia).
evidence: Split compound verbs into prefix and stem and infer their meaning
Recognise assimilated prefixes (affero, colloquor, imprimo)
Derive the meaning of nouns and adjectives from known stems and common suffixes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Without a dictionary, can {{name}} work out what 'reducere' and 'amicitia' mean from words they know?

prerequisites.reason: Word parts are recognised in known vocabulary
Prefixes and suffixes are known from German word formation
The idea of word families is known from German

osMatches.note: os: using Latin roots for English vocabulary

topics.subject: Latein
topics.name: Using a Latin Dictionary
topics.nameDe: Lateinisches Wörterbuch nutzen und Bedeutungen wählen
topics.description: Use a Latin–German dictionary (e.g. Stowasser, PONS, Langenscheidt) for original texts: trace a form back to its dictionary entry, read the entry's grammar information and choose the meaning that fits the context (Monosemierung).
evidence: Find the dictionary form of inflected words, including perfect stems and compound verbs
Use the grammatical information of an entry (case government, constructions)
Choose between meanings of polysemous words such as petere, res or ratio by context
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} meets 'pacem petivit' in a text, can they find 'petere' in the dictionary and choose 'um Frieden bitten' rather than 'angreifen'?

prerequisites.reason: Finding the entry requires recognising perfect stems
Compound verbs must be split to be found
Basic dictionary skills were learnt in English

topics.laenderNotes: A dictionary is normally allowed in Latin class tests from the start of the reading phase and in the Abitur; the Latinum exam also allows one.

topics.subject: Latein
topics.name: First and Second Declension
topics.description: Decline nouns of the a-declension (amica) and o-declension (amicus, puer, ager, templum) in all cases including the ablative and vocative, and identify the case and number of a form in a sentence.
evidence: Decline a-, o- and neuter o-declension nouns in all cases
Name all possible cases of an ambiguous form (amicae, templa)
Identify the case of nouns in a simple sentence and translate accordingly
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you which cases 'amicis' could be and decide which one fits in 'Marcus amicis librum dat'?

prerequisites.reason: Case is a familiar concept from German
Declining noun groups is practised in German
Number is a familiar category

topics.subject: Latein
topics.name: Present Tense of Latin Verbs
topics.nameDe: Präsens der Konjugationen, esse, Infinitiv und Imperativ
topics.description: Conjugate verbs of the a-, e-, i-, consonant and mixed conjugations and the verb esse in the present active, form infinitive and imperative, and recognise the subject from the personal ending.
evidence: Conjugate verbs of all conjugation classes and esse in the present tense
Translate the personal ending as the hidden subject (vocat = er/sie/es ruft)
Form and translate infinitives and imperatives (vocare, voca!, vocate!)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} translate 'audimus' and 'veniunt' without help and say which endings show the person?

prerequisites.reason: Person and number on the verb are known from German
The word class verb is known

topics.subject: Latein
topics.name: Adjectives and KNG Agreement
topics.description: Decline adjectives of the a/o-declension (bonus, bona, bonum; liber, pulcher) and use KNG agreement (case, number, gender) to find which noun an adjective belongs to, even when they are separated in the sentence.
evidence: Decline adjectives in all three genders
Match adjectives to their nouns by KNG agreement, also with different endings (agricola bonus)
Distinguish attributive and predicative use (Prädikatsnomen with esse)
topics.assessmentPrompt: In 'Magnam villam pulchram videmus', can {{name}} explain that both adjectives belong to 'villam' by checking case, number and gender?

prerequisites.reason: Adjectives use the same endings as a/o-nouns
The word class adjective is known from German

topics.subject: Latein
topics.name: Personal, Possessive and Reflexive Pronouns
topics.description: Use the personal pronouns (ego, tu, nos, vos), the possessives (meus, tuus, noster, vester) and the reflexives se and suus, which refer back to the subject, unlike eius and eorum.
evidence: Decline the personal pronouns and translate their forms
Translate possessives that agree with the thing possessed
Distinguish suus (refers to the subject) from eius (refers to someone else)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain the difference between 'Marcus amicum suum videt' and 'Marcus amicum eius videt'?

prerequisites.reason: Possessives decline like adjectives
Personal pronouns are known from German

topics.subject: Latein
topics.name: Third Declension
topics.description: Decline third-declension nouns (rex, regis; corpus, corporis; urbs, urbis) and adjectives (fortis, acer, felix), whose stem appears only in the genitive, and keep apart endings that look like a/o-declension forms.
evidence: Find the stem of a third-declension noun from its genitive
Decline consonant and i-stem nouns and third-declension adjectives
Avoid confusing endings across declensions (e.g. -is, -es, -um, -a)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} decline 'nomen, nominis' and explain why 'nomina' is a plural and not a feminine singular?

prerequisites.reason: The case system is first learnt with the a/o-declension
The genitive in the learning form gives the stem

topics.subject: Latein
topics.name: Imperfect and Future Tense
topics.description: Form and recognise the imperfect (-ba-) and the future I (-b- for a/e-conjugation, -a-/-e- for the others) of all conjugations and esse, and use the imperfect for background and repeated past actions.
evidence: Form the imperfect and future of all conjugations and of esse (eram, ero)
Distinguish future forms of the consonant conjugation (reget) from present forms (regit)
Translate the imperfect appropriately in a narrative
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you whether 'audiet', 'audiebat' and 'audit' refer to the present, past or future?

prerequisites.reason: Tenses are built on the present stem
The German Präteritum is the translation of the imperfect
The German Futur is known

topics.subject: Latein
topics.name: Perfect-Stem Tenses and Principal Parts
topics.nameDe: Perfektstamm: Perfekt, Plusquamperfekt, Futur II und Stammformen
topics.description: Form the perfect active with its typical stem changes (v-, u-, s-perfect, lengthening, reduplication, no change) and learn the principal parts; build the pluperfect and future perfect on the same stem, and translate the perfect as the main narrative past and the other two as anteriority.
evidence: Name the perfect stem type of common verbs (laudavi, monui, scripsi, veni, dedi) and trace forms back to the dictionary form
